title: The Institute Founded Twice: Zuffenhausen, Morningside Heights, Montagnola
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Zuffenhausen, born in the manufacturer's house
stops.date_confidence: attested; day and place from the Frankfurt University Library archival chronology, confirmed by the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. No birth-house address survives in the reachable record, so the pin marks the Zuffenhausen town centre.
stops.campa: Zuffenhausen is a separate town north of Stuttgart, annexed to the city only in 1931, and on the fourteenth of February a son is born there to Moritz Horkheimer, textile manufacturer, and his wife Babette, born Lauchheimer. The house is Jewish and prosperous and has its succession settled in advance: the boy is the only son, and the mills are meant for him. His father begins at once to plan the commercial education that will hand the firm over intact. The boy is named Max. No address for the birth house survives.
suggested_refs: Zuffenhausen before its 1931 annexation to Stuttgart
The Horkheimer textile works of the Stuttgart region

stops.name: Stuttgart, the Gymnasium left for the factory
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the fact, inferred as to month; the Frankfurt archival chronology gives 1910/11 for the departure from the Gymnasium without further precision. Coordinates mark the historic city centre; no factory address was recovered.
stops.campa: At sixteen he leaves the Stuttgart Gymnasium without the Abitur and enters his father's textile works as a trainee, then as a junior manager. The commercial formation includes training journeys through Belgium, France, and England, the trade routes of the firm rather than the routes of a student. In these years he meets Friedrich Pollock, a manufacturer's son like himself, and the friendship holds for the next six decades. Neither of them wants the business they are being handed. They read Schopenhauer and write fiction on the side.
suggested_refs: The commercial training journeys through Belgium, France and England, named only by country in the archival chronology

stops.name: Zuffenhausen, the war and the sanatorium
stops.date_confidence: contested. German Wikipedia: conscripted spring 1917, months in a Munich sanatorium with a lung illness, discharged spring 1918 on medical grounds. English Wikipedia says instead that he avoided service, was rejected on medical grounds, and failed an army physical before enrolling in spring 1919. The two accounts are not reconciled here. No unit, diagnosis, or exact date is established in any reachable source.
stops.campa: Conscripted in the spring of 1917, he spends months in a Munich sanatorium with a lung illness and is discharged the following spring on medical grounds. He sees no combat and wins no decoration, and he returns to the family factory while the front collapses. The English record tells it differently, saying he avoided service and failed an army physical outright. Either way the war passes over him and leaves the heir in the counting house. No unit and no diagnosis are recorded on either account.
suggested_refs: John Abromeit's caution against overstating the draft-avoidance version of these months

stops.name: Munich, the Abitur at twenty-four
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year and city; month inferred from the spring 1919 enrolment given in the chronology.
stops.campa: The empire falls and the succession falls with it. He takes an external Abitur in Munich, the school certificate he had walked away from at sixteen, and enrols at the Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität in the spring of 1919 to read philosophy, psychology, and economics. The textile firm will keep running without its heir. What he wants from a university is not yet a career but a vocabulary for what the war and the revolution have just done to the country he grew up rich in. Pollock enrols beside him. He is twenty-four years old and a first-year student.
suggested_refs: The external Abitur examination taken in Munich after the imperial collapse

stops.name: Munich, taken for Ernst Toller
stops.date_confidence: tradition. Stated as fact in Wikipedia citing the standard biographies and well attested in the literature (Wiggershaus, Abromeit), but no arrest file, date, detention site, or duration has been located. Month assigned only to place the episode inside the collapse of the council republic.
stops.campa: Munich in the spring of 1919 is a council republic under siege, and the authorities are hunting the writers who declared it. They take Horkheimer for Ernst Toller, the revolutionary playwright, and hold him briefly before letting him go. No charge follows and no arrest register has been found; the story reaches us through the biographers rather than through a police file. What is certain is that he was in the city while the Freikorps retook it, and that he was mistaken, for an afternoon, for someone worth shooting.
suggested_refs: Ernst Toller's own account of the Munich council republic and its suppression

stops.name: Freiburg im Breisgau, two semesters of Husserl and Heidegger
stops.date_confidence: attested for winter semester 1920/21 through summer semester 1921 in the Frankfurt archival chronology; month set to the opening of the winter term. That Horkheimer personally attended particular Husserl or Heidegger lectures rests on the chronology, not on a class register.
stops.campa: For the winter semester of 1920 and the summer that follows he and Pollock move to Freiburg, where Edmund Husserl holds the chair in philosophy and a young assistant named Martin Heidegger is lecturing. Horkheimer sits in both rooms. Neither man will figure in his later work as a teacher he owns; phenomenology strikes him as a method that brackets away exactly the history he wants explained. He leaves after two semesters for Frankfurt and Hans Cornelius, a Kantian who taught painting and music as readily as logic.
suggested_refs: The Freiburg lecture lists for winter 1920/21 and summer 1921

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the doctorate on teleological judgment
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year, title, and supervisor; month unknown and defaulted. Pin is the Campus Bockenheim, where Horkheimer studied, habilitated and later held his chair.
stops.campa: He abandons a project in Gestalt psychology and writes instead on Kant: Zur Antinomie der teleologischen Urteilskraft, on the antinomy of teleological judgment, submitted to Hans Cornelius in 1922. The question is whether nature can be thought as purposive without the thought becoming a claim about nature itself. Horkheimer will spend forty years asking a version of the same question about reason, whether it can hold an end of its own or only serve one. Kant's own answer is that the purposiveness is a regulative principle and not a fact about nature.
suggested_refs: Kant, Kritik der Urteilskraft, the antinomy of teleological judgment

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the habilitation on the third Critique
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year and title; month unknown and defaulted. The venia legendi and the Privatdozent appointment are given as 1925/26 across sources.
stops.campa: Three years later he habilitates, again under Cornelius, again on the Critique of Judgment, this time as the hinge between the theoretical and the practical philosophy: Über Kants Kritik der Urteilskraft als Bindeglied zwischen theoretischer und praktischer Philosophie. The venia legendi follows and he becomes Privatdozent. The Institute for Social Research has been standing on the Viktoria-Allee since 1924, financed out of a Buenos Aires grain fortune, and he has nothing to do with it. He is thirty-one and unsalaried.
suggested_refs: Hans Cornelius, Transcendentale Systematik, the Kantian frame Horkheimer worked inside as a student

stops.name: Kronberg im Taunus, the marriage against the house
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year and place, LEO-BW recording the marriage at Cronberg am Taunus in 1926; month unknown and defaulted. Her birth year is contested: English and German Wikipedia make her eight years his senior, born 1887; the Baden-Württemberg genealogy gives 1897 and stands alone.
stops.campa: He marries Rosa Christine Riekher, called Maidon, at Kronberg im Taunus. She had been his father's personal secretary and she is Christian. His parents had opposed the match for years as a mesalliance beneath the house, and he marries her anyway; they stay married until she dies in 1969 and they have no children. In time they keep a house at Kronberg together with Pollock, the friend from the factory years. Most sources make her eight years his senior, born in 1887, and the Baden-Württemberg genealogy gives 1897 instead. No civil certificate has been consulted to settle which.
suggested_refs: LEO-BW genealogical record of the 1926 marriage at Cronberg am Taunus

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the chair and the directorship
stops.date_confidence: attested: professorship in July 1930, directorship in October. Sources differ on whether to date the whole appointment 1929, 1930 or 1931, and felix_weil.journey.json records the German date as 1931. Pin inherited byte-identical from felix_weil.journey.json.
stops.campa: Carl Grünberg, the Institute's founding director, has had a stroke, and Pollock holds the post provisionally. In July the ministry appoints Horkheimer to a newly endowed chair in social philosophy, and in October, at Felix Weil's instigation, he takes the directorship. Weil founded the Institute in 1923 and pays for it out of Weil Hermanos y Cia, his father's grain house in Buenos Aires. The university gives him standing and the Argentine money gives him a staff. Sources put the whole appointment variously in 1929, in 1930 and in 1931.
suggested_refs: Weil Hermanos y Cia, Buenos Aires, founded 1898, the grain house that endowed the Institute
The First Marxist Work Week at Geraberg, Thuringia, 20 May 1923, which Karl Korsch conceived, Weil financed and Richard Sorge convened
sources: Historical Materialism, interview with Hans-Peter Gruber on Felix Weil
felix_weil.journey.json, stop 'Frankfurt am Main, Horkheimer takes the chair'

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the inaugural lecture
stops.date_confidence: attested; full date given in the Stanford entry and the Institute's own centenary history.
stops.campa: On the twenty-fourth of January he reads his inaugural lecture in the university aula and describes what he intends the Institute to become: not a chair with assistants but a permanent apparatus in which philosophers, economists, sociologists, psychologists and historians work the same material at once, each discipline correcting the others. Social philosophy alone cannot say what a society is doing to the people inside it. Neither can a survey. The lecture is a work order, and he will spend thirty years filling it. He is thirty-five years old and has held the directorship for three months.
stops.quote: Its ultimate aim is the philosophical interpretation of the vicissitudes of human fate.
stops.quote_source: Max Horkheimer, 'The Present Situation of Social Philosophy and the Tasks of an Institute for Social Research,' inaugural lecture, Frankfurt, 24 January 1931
suggested_refs: Die gegenwärtige Lage der Sozialphilosophie und die Aufgaben eines Instituts für Sozialforschung (1931)
sources: Institut für Sozialforschung centenary history, ifs.uni-frankfurt.de/schlaglichter.html

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the Zeitschrift and the Freudian instrument
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year of founding; month unknown and defaulted. Fromm's entry into the Institute is dated 1930 in erich_fromm.journey.json. Pin inherited byte-identical from felix_weil.journey.json.
stops.campa: He founds the Zeitschrift für Sozialforschung and edits it himself, and it becomes the organ where the program is actually executed. Erich Fromm runs the social psychology, and the instrument he brings is Sigmund Freud: the question of why the German working class does not act as its interests would predict, put to workers directly, in questionnaires, and counted. The answers come back and they are bad. The regime those answers predicted arrives within the year, and the study waits four decades for a publisher.
stops.quote: the question today is to organize investigations stimulated by contemporary philosophical problems
stops.quote_source: Max Horkheimer, 'The Present Situation of Social Philosophy and the Tasks of an Institute for Social Research,' inaugural lecture of 24 January 1931, describing the program the Zeitschrift was founded to execute
suggested_refs: Erich Fromm's Weimar worker study, completed c. 1931, unpublished until the 1980s
The Zeitschrift für Sozialforschung, complete run 1932-1941
sources: Institut für Sozialforschung centenary history, ifs.uni-frankfurt.de/schlaglichter.html
erich_fromm.journey.json, stop 'Frankfurt, the Institute for Social Research'

stops.name: Kronberg im Taunus, the SA at the door
stops.date_confidence: attested to January 1933 in the Institute chronology and Wiggershaus; no day recorded, month day defaulted.
stops.campa: In January SA men occupy the house at Kronberg that Horkheimer shares with Pollock. Hitler has been chancellor for days and the machinery of the state has not yet been assembled, but the men who come to the door are not waiting for it. Horkheimer has already begun moving the Institute's assets out of Germany, months before this, and the occupation of a private house in the Taunus tells him the calculation was right. He does not go back to the house.
suggested_refs: The Horkheimer-Pollock residence at Kronberg im Taunus
sources: Rolf Wiggershaus, Die Frankfurter Schule, as summarised in the consulted chronology

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the building taken
stops.date_confidence: attested in sequence: police closure March, transfer to the Nazi student organisation May, Gestapo record of closure for subversive activities July. Day within March not recorded. Pin inherited byte-identical from felix_weil.journey.json.
stops.campa: The police close the Institute in March. In May the building passes to the National Socialist student organisation, and in July the Gestapo enters the closure formally, for subversive activities. Horkheimer is dismissed from the university under the legislation that removes Jews from the civil service, one name on a list that empties Frankfurt of its faculty. The library and the endowment are already out of the country. The house Franz Roeckle built in 1924 will stand until Allied bombers destroy it in 1944.
suggested_refs: Franz Roeckle's Institute building on the Viktoria-Allee, opened 22 June 1924, destroyed by bombing in 1944
sources: Institut für Sozialforschung history page, ifs.uni-frankfurt.de

stops.name: Geneva, the foundation that held the money
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the Geneva base and the Société Internationale de Recherches Sociales; month inferred. Pin inherited byte-identical from felix_weil.journey.json, stop 'Geneva, the Société Internationale de Recherches Sociales'. No Geneva street address for Horkheimer himself was located.
stops.campa: The Société Internationale de Recherches Sociales, seated in Geneva, is where Felix Weil had put the endowment before the German state could reach it, and it is now the Institute. Horkheimer directs from the city while branch offices open in Paris and London and the Zeitschrift is printed abroad. What has been preserved is not a building but a payroll. The staff is scattered and the country is shut behind them, and the money is Argentine, held in Switzerland, out of reach of the German state.
suggested_refs: The Société Internationale de Recherches Sociales, Geneva, the legal shell of the exiled Institute
sources: felix_weil.journey.json, stop 'Geneva, the Société Internationale de Recherches Sociales'

stops.name: Zurich, Dämmerung under a false name
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year, place of publication and pseudonym in the Frankfurt bibliography; month unknown and defaulted. Whether Horkheimer was personally in Zurich for the publication is not established.
stops.campa: His aphorisms of the Weimar years appear in Zurich as Dämmerung: Notizen in Deutschland, signed Heinrich Regius. He is thirty-nine, out of his country, running an institute out of a Swiss foundation and publishing his own notes on Germany under a name that is not his. The pseudonym is not a literary pose. People named in the book, and people who could be traced through it to its author, are still inside Germany and still reachable. The German title means dawn and dusk at once, and declines to say which one is meant.
suggested_refs: Heinrich Regius, Dämmerung: Notizen in Deutschland (Zurich: Oprecht und Helbling, 1934)

stops.name: New York, Columbia takes the Institute in
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year and premises; month inferred. erich_fromm.journey.json dates Fromm's own crossing to 31 May 1934. Pin inherited byte-identical from felix_weil.journey.json, stop 'New York, Columbia takes the institute in'.
stops.campa: Nicholas Murray Butler, president of Columbia, offers the exiled Institute affiliation and a building at 429 West 117th Street, and the principal centre moves to Morningside Heights. Horkheimer, Pollock, Adorno, Marcuse, Löwenthal and Erich Fromm cross. They keep the name, the director, the Geneva endowment and, for six more years, the German language of the journal. Felix Weil, whose money it is, does not travel with them. An American university has taken in a Marxist research institute and given it a street address.
suggested_refs: 429 West 117th Street, New York, the Institute's American premises
sources: felix_weil.journey.json, stop 'New York, Columbia takes the institute in'
erich_fromm.journey.json, stop 'Columbia University, arrival on the thirty-first of May'

stops.name: New York, Authority and the Family
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year and contributors; month unknown and defaulted. The volume was printed in Paris by Félix Alcan for the New York Institute, so the pin marks where it was made rather than where it was set in type.
stops.campa: Studien über Autorität und Familie appears from the exiled Institute, nine hundred pages, edited by Horkheimer with the theoretical sections his own and the major contributions from Erich Fromm and Herbert Marcuse. The question is how a family manufactures the character that submits, and it is asked while the answer is being demonstrated across the Atlantic. The book is printed in Paris, in German, for readers who mostly cannot get it. It is the last large collective work the Institute completes with Fromm inside it.
suggested_refs: Studien über Autorität und Familie (Paris: Félix Alcan, 1936)

stops.name: New York, traditional and critical theory
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year and journal; month unknown and defaulted.
stops.campa: Traditionelle und kritische Theorie appears in the Zeitschrift, with a postscript written together with Marcuse, and it names the thing the Institute has been doing since 1931. Traditional theory takes its object as given and itself as neutral. Critical theory knows it is produced by the society it examines and aims at that society's alteration. Max Weber had described the rationality that calculates means and asks nothing about ends; Horkheimer gives that rationality a history and a class position. The term critical theory dates from this essay.
stops.quote: Philosophy insists that the actions and aims of man must not be the product of blind necessity.
stops.quote_source: Max Horkheimer, 'The Social Function of Philosophy' (1939), written two years after the essay this stop marks
suggested_refs: Traditionelle und kritische Theorie, Zeitschrift für Sozialforschung VI/2 (1937), with the Marcuse postscript

stops.name: Paris, the last meeting with Benjamin
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the 1937 European trip and the meeting; month inferred, venue not established. Pin is the canonical Paris pin inherited byte-identical from felix_weil.journey.json.
stops.campa: He returns briefly to Europe and meets Walter Benjamin in Paris. The Institute pays Benjamin a stipend, which is most of what he lives on, and Horkheimer and Adorno send his manuscripts back with demands for revision that Benjamin accepts and resents. The relationship is rescue and editorship at once, and neither man can separate the two. Benjamin will die at Portbou in 1940 with an exit visa that arrived a day late. This is the last time the two of them are in a room together.
suggested_refs: The Adorno-Horkheimer Briefwechsel (Suhrkamp, 2003-2006), on the Institute's editorial handling of Benjamin

stops.name: New York, the Jews and Europe
stops.date_confidence: attested as to essay, journal, volume and page; month unknown and defaulted. The English wording that circulates for the quoted sentence is a common rendering and not a published translation, so the German is given here and the English only as a gloss.
stops.campa: Die Juden und Europa appears in the Zeitschrift, and its argument is that fascism is not a lapse from liberal capitalism but a form capitalism takes when it needs one. It is also a rebuke to the emigration around him, which wants to believe the regime is a barbarism standing outside history rather than an outcome standing inside it. The sentence everyone afterwards remembers is the shortest in the essay. He writes it in New York, in German, for a journal read by a few hundred exiles. It stands in volume eight, at page 115.
stops.quote: Wer aber vom Kapitalismus nicht reden will, sollte auch vom Faschismus schweigen.
stops.quote_source: Max Horkheimer, 'Die Juden und Europa,' Zeitschrift für Sozialforschung vol. 8 (New York, 1939), p. 115. Gloss: whoever is not willing to talk about capitalism should also remain silent about fascism.
suggested_refs: Die Juden und Europa, Zeitschrift für Sozialforschung VIII (1939)
sources: de.wikiquote.org, 'Max Horkheimer', citing the 1939 Zeitschrift text with page

stops.name: New York, the social function of philosophy
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the 1939 essay; month inferred. The English text is the one Horkheimer published, not a translation.
stops.campa: He lectures and publishes on what philosophy is for, and answers that it is not for supplying certainties and not for supervising the sciences. Its function is to refuse the settled terms in which a society describes itself. Science has a criterion outside itself, its own success at prediction and control; philosophy has none, and that lack is not a defect but the condition of its office. The essay runs in Studies in Philosophy and Social Science, the English-language continuation of the Zeitschrift. He is writing in English now.
stops.quote: The real social function of philosophy lies in its criticism of what is prevalent.
stops.quote_source: Max Horkheimer, 'The Social Function of Philosophy' (1939)
suggested_refs: The Social Function of Philosophy, Studies in Philosophy and Social Science VIII (1939)

stops.name: New York, Fromm leaves
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the 1939 departure and the financial settlement; month inferred. The dossier's further claim that later Institute-centred histories deliberately minimised Fromm is contested and is not treated as established here.
stops.campa: Erich Fromm leaves the Institute under a financial settlement. The stated ground is money: the endowment has contracted and the payroll has to shrink. Underneath it are years of theoretical divergence, Fromm moving away from Freud's drive theory toward the social character, Adorno rising in Horkheimer's estimation and pressing against him. Fromm's Weimar worker study stays unpublished, and he does not cross back into the Institute again. No single-cause account of the break holds up in the record as it stands.
suggested_refs: Neil McLaughlin, 'Origin Myths in the Social Sciences,' on the historiography of the Fromm break
Erich Fromm Papers finding aid, New York Public Library, archives.nypl.org/mss/1090

stops.name: Pacific Palisades, citizenship and the move west
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1940 by English Wikipedia for both the citizenship and the move; month inferred. Some accounts give 1941 for the move, which contradicts the 1940-1949 span the geography record itself carries. No street address for Horkheimer's own house was located.
stops.campa: He becomes a citizen of the United States and moves west to Pacific Palisades, above the ocean, for his health and for the quiet. The German-speaking emigration is already there and around it: Thomas Mann on San Remo Drive, Lion Feuchtwanger at the Villa Aurora, Schoenberg over in Brentwood, Brecht in Santa Monica. Adorno follows him out. The two of them begin working every day in the same room, and the arrangement holds without a break for the next four years.
stops.quote: Films, radio and magazines make up a system which is uniform as a whole and in every part.
stops.quote_source: Max Horkheimer and Theodor W. Adorno, 'The Culture Industry: Enlightenment as Mass Deception,' written in Los Angeles between 1942 and 1944; co-authored, not solely Horkheimer's
suggested_refs: The Villa Aurora, Pacific Palisades, and the Los Angeles German emigration of the 1940s

stops.name: Pacific Palisades, the Philosophische Fragmente
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1942-1944 drafting and the 1944 mimeograph; month unknown and defaulted. The culture-industry chapter is jointly authored with Adorno and the quoted sentence is not solely Horkheimer's.
stops.campa: They dictate to each other and to Gretel Adorno, who types and keeps the notes and whose contribution a preface will finally acknowledge in 1969. What comes out in mimeograph in 1944 as Philosophische Fragmente asks how enlightenment, which set out to free people from myth by explaining the world, produced a world that administers them. The chapter on the culture industry is written in Los Angeles, within driving distance of the studios, by two men who read the newspapers and go to the pictures.
stops.quote: The culture industry perpetually cheats its consumers of what it perpetually promises.
stops.quote_source: Max Horkheimer and Theodor W. Adorno, 'The Culture Industry: Enlightenment as Mass Deception,' Dialectic of Enlightenment (drafted Los Angeles 1942-1944)
suggested_refs: Philosophische Fragmente, mimeographed by the Institute of Social Research, New York, 1944

stops.name: New York, the American Jewish Committee
stops.date_confidence: contested start date: sources give 1942 and 1943/44 for the administrative appointment, and the project runs to 1949. Month unknown and defaulted. Coordinates mark the AJC's historic Manhattan headquarters area rather than a confirmed office.
stops.campa: He takes the scientific direction of the American Jewish Committee's research department on antisemitism and plans the volumes that appear as Studies in Prejudice. The largest of them, The Authoritarian Personality, puts Adorno and a team of Berkeley psychologists to work building a scale that measures the disposition to submit and to punish. The Institute that could not get its Weimar worker study into print is now paid by an American organisation to ask the same question in English. Sources give 1942 and 1943 for the appointment and do not agree. The project runs until 1949.
suggested_refs: Studies in Prejudice, five volumes, American Jewish Committee, 1949-1950

stops.name: New York, the Columbia lectures on reason
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the 1944 Columbia lectures and the 1947 book; month inferred. The quoted sentence is confirmed with a page citation through a secondary source, the Internet Archive copy exposing no readable text; it should be checked against a printed copy before being treated as fully attested.
stops.campa: He lectures at Columbia on reason and publishes the lectures in 1947 as Eclipse of Reason, the argument of Dialectic of Enlightenment carried into the language of an American lecture hall. The distinction it turns on is between objective reason, which asks what ends are worth pursuing, and subjective or instrumental reason, which asks only how efficiently a given end may be reached and takes the end from whoever is paying. A reason that cannot judge ends will serve any of them. It is the first book he writes in English.
stops.quote: Reason has never really directed social reality, but now reason has been so thoroughly purged of any specific trend or preference that it has finally renounced even the task of passing judgment on man's actions and way of life.
stops.quote_source: Max Horkheimer, Eclipse of Reason (New York: Oxford University Press, 1947), p. 9
suggested_refs: Eclipse of Reason (Oxford University Press, 1947), from the 1944 Columbia lectures

stops.name: Amsterdam, Querido on the Keizersgracht
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year, city and publisher; month unknown and defaulted. This stop marks the book's place of publication and not Horkheimer's travel, which is not established. Coordinates are Keizersgracht 333, the Querido exile house.
stops.campa: Querido, the German-language exile house at Keizersgracht 333, prints Dialektik der Aufklärung: Philosophische Fragmente with Horkheimer's name first on the title page. The firm had published Döblin and the Manns through the thirties and had been shut down under the occupation; this is one of its last acts in that line. Twenty years on, students who were not born when it was written will carry it through the German universities, against the stated politics of both its authors. On publication it sells almost nothing.
suggested_refs: Querido Verlag, Keizersgracht 333, Amsterdam, the German exile imprint

stops.name: New York, the Rockefeller passage back
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to the planning venue: April 1948 is given for the first postwar return trip, but no meeting location is documented, and the coordinates mark the Rockefeller Center area associated with the Foundation's historic New York offices.
stops.campa: With Rockefeller Foundation support he sails for Europe in April, the first return since 1933, and goes to Frankfurt to see what is there. The city is rubble, the university is improvising, and the Institute building was destroyed by bombing four years earlier. German colleagues who stayed put through the whole of it receive him correctly. He is fifty-three, an American citizen with a chair waiting for him in a country that dismissed him. Pollock advises against going back at all.
suggested_refs: The Rockefeller Foundation grant supporting the 1948 European research trip

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the chair restored
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1949 for the return and the restoration of the professorship; month inferred.
stops.campa: He returns to Germany and the university restores his chair. The legal instrument is restitution, and what restitution restores is a title, a salary and a room; the students who would have filled the seminar in 1933 are not available for restoration. He teaches philosophy and sociology to a generation that was in the Hitler Youth. He does not make speeches about this. He rebuilds the Institute instead. The money comes from the Americans, from the city and from private donors, and the work takes two years.
stops.quote: Reason is a poor ally of reaction.
stops.quote_source: Max Horkheimer, 'The Social Function of Philosophy' (1939), written in New York ten years before this return
suggested_refs: The West German Wiedergutmachung provisions under which dismissed professors were reinstated

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the new house on the Senckenberganlage
stops.date_confidence: attested; the reopening date of 14 November 1951 is inherited from felix_weil.journey.json, stop 'Frankfurt am Main, the institute reopens', along with the pin, byte-identical.
stops.campa: The Institute reopens on the fourteenth of November in a new building on the Senckenberganlage, near the ground where Roeckle's house stood until the bombing. The money comes from John J. McCloy's High Commission fund, from the city of Frankfurt and from private donors; Felix Weil, whose fortune built the first one, is in America and no longer rich. Horkheimer is director again, with Pollock and Adorno back beside him. He has now founded the same institute twice in one lifetime, in the same street.
suggested_refs: The bronze relief in the entrance hall of the rebuilt Institute
John J. McCloy's High Commission reconstruction fund
sources: felix_weil.journey.json, stop 'Frankfurt am Main, the institute reopens'

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, rector of the university
stops.date_confidence: attested for the rectorate of 1951-1953; month inferred so as to fall after the Institute reopening of 14 November.
stops.campa: He is elected rector of the University of Frankfurt and serves two years, the first Jew to hold the office in its postwar history. The work is reconstruction: buildings, appointments, budgets, the Western democratic integration of a university that had expelled its own faculty eighteen years earlier. The man who wrote that critical theory aims at the alteration of society is now signing the payroll of a West German state institution. He does the administrative job carefully and he is re-elected to it.
suggested_refs: The Frankfurt rectorate records for 1951-1953

stops.name: Düsseldorf, the Mannesmann study
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The commission is reported in Institute institutional histories but the primary contract record was not retrieved. Month unknown and defaulted. The reading that the study was meant to forestall socialist organising is an interpretation and not a demonstrated clause.
stops.campa: The Institute contracts to study the workforce at Mannesmann, a steel and tube firm that armed the Reich and used forced labour under Wilhelm Zangen, who is back in business. Empirical sociology in the Federal Republic is paid for by the firms it surveys, and the Institute needs both the money and the access to the shop floor. Whether the commission was meant to head off organising among the workers is an interpretation, not a clause anyone has produced. Horkheimer takes the work.
suggested_refs: The Institute's industrial-sociology commissions of the 1950s and their corporate funders
sources: Institute institutional histories as synthesised in the consulted dossier; primary contract record not retrieved

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the chair given up
stops.date_confidence: contested. The university retirement is dated 1959; the transfer of the Institute's practical direction to Adorno is given as 1958 or as a staged handover, and the sources are not reconciled. Month inferred.
stops.campa: He retires from the chair in 1959, having handed the day-to-day direction of the Institute to Adorno over the preceding years; whether that transfer happened in 1958 or in stages, the sources do not agree. He had also been crossing to Chicago through the middle of the decade as a visiting professor, keeping one foot in the country whose passport he carries. The Institute he leaves behind is respectable, funded and about to be adopted by a student movement he will not recognise.
suggested_refs: The University of Chicago visiting professorships of the mid-1950s, semesters and course titles not established

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the Römer: the plaque and the citizenship
stops.date_confidence: attested as to both awards; the Goethe Plaque is dated 1953 by the university archive's award list and 1951 by popular accounts, and the archive is preferred here without the contradiction being resolved. Month unknown and defaulted. The Römer is the presumed ceremonial site and is not separately confirmed.
stops.campa: The city gives him the Goethe Plaque in 1953, though popular accounts move it to 1951, and in 1960 makes him an honorary citizen of Frankfurt for life. Both are conferred at the Römer, the old city hall rebuilt out of its own ashes. The award list in the university archive is the only document that settles the plaque's date, and it settles it against the more repeated version. He is honoured for having come back, which is the thing the city most needs to be able to say about itself. He accepts both.

stops.name: Montagnola, the house above the lake
stops.date_confidence: contested. The detailed Deutsche Biographie and LEO-BW chronology favours 1957; the Frankfurt archive's short chronology associates the move with 1959. Both are recorded, 1957 used here for ordering. Month unknown and defaulted.
stops.campa: Max and Maidon settle increasingly at Montagnola in the Ticino, above the Lugano lake, with Pollock nearby. The official short chronology puts the move in 1959 and the detailed one in 1957. What he writes here is notes rather than books, and the revolutionary horizon of the thirties has gone out of them; what stands in its place is resistance without expectation and a longing he will not name except negatively. He keeps the German ties and crosses back for lectures.
suggested_refs: The Horkheimer house at Montagnola, Ticino

stops.name: Montagnola, theism and atheism
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the 1963 essay; month unknown and defaulted. The pin is his residence, not a documented place of composition.
stops.campa: Theismus und Atheismus, published in 1963, argues that the two positions have exchanged their contents. Theology once justified power; the atheism that opposed it has become the common sense of an administered world and justifies power in its turn. What he wants from the theological is not a doctrine and not a consolation but a name for the possibility that the murdered are not simply gone. He is sixty-eight and no longer arguing for a rational society. He is arguing that without something like God the word meaning cannot be held to anything at all.
stops.quote: Without God one will try in vain to preserve absolute meaning.
suggested_refs: Theismus und Atheismus (1963), in Zur Kritik der instrumentellen Vernunft

stops.name: Montagnola, the year the losses cluster
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the deaths of Maidon and Adorno in 1969 and Pollock in 1970; month assigned only to order the segment. Maidon's place of death is not established in any reachable source.
stops.campa: Maidon dies in 1969, forty-three years married. Adorno dies the same year in the Valais, of a heart attack, after a term in which students had disrupted his classes. Pollock, the friend from the textile years, dies in 1970. Horkheimer is seventy-four and the three people who constituted his working life are gone inside eighteen months. Where Maidon died is not recorded in the sources reachable here; the burial is at Bern, in the plot he had already written to the cemetery commission to ask for.
suggested_refs: Horkheimer's letter to the Bern cemetery commission requesting burial beside his wife and near his parents

stops.name: Montagnola, the longing for the wholly other
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the 1970 interview volume and its Hamburg publisher, Furche-Verlag; month unknown and inferred. The interview was conducted with Hellmut Gumnior; the pin is Horkheimer's residence rather than a documented interview venue.
stops.campa: Hellmut Gumnior interviews him at length and Furche-Verlag publishes the result in Hamburg as Die Sehnsucht nach dem ganz Anderen, the longing for the wholly other. In it he takes the side of Paul VI against artificial contraception, on the ground that the pill will make sexuality administrable and put an end to love, a position his readers on the left cannot follow him to and one he does not withdraw. The book is the most widely read thing he publishes after the war.
stops.quote: Theology has always tried to reconcile the demands of the Gospels and of power.
stops.quote_source: Max Horkheimer, 'Theism and Atheism' (1963), seven years before the Gumnior interview
suggested_refs: Die Sehnsucht nach dem ganz Anderen, interview with Hellmut Gumnior (Hamburg: Furche-Verlag, 1970)

stops.name: Stuttgart, the Citizens' Medal and the Lessing Prize
stops.date_confidence: attested as to both awards and their years, 1970 and 1971, in the university archive's award list; months unknown and inferred. The Rathaus is the presumed civic site for the Stuttgart medal and is not separately confirmed; the Hamburg ceremony venue is likewise unrecorded.
stops.campa: Stuttgart, the city his father's mills fed and the city whose Gymnasium he walked out of at sixteen, gives him its Citizens' Medal in 1970. Hamburg gives him the Lessing Prize the following year. He is seventy-five and seventy-six respectively, and the honours come from German cities to a man who spent sixteen years out of the country because German cities had let him be driven from it. The award list records the dates and nothing about the ceremonies.

stops.name: Nuremberg, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested as to date and city. No cause of death and no clinic is established in any consulted source; the account that the death followed a routine medical examination is unverified. Coordinates mark central Nuremberg.
stops.campa: He dies at Nuremberg on the seventh of July, seventy-eight years old. He had been born in a Württemberg textile town under an emperor and dies in a Federal Republic he had helped to teach how to describe itself. His last completed work is a book of interviews, and the Institute he founded twice is standing on the Senckenberganlage. Some accounts have the death following a routine medical examination. No cause is established in anything reachable here, and no clinic is named.

stops.name: Bern, the Jewish cemetery on the Papiermühlestrasse
stops.date_confidence: attested as to burial place; the day of the funeral is inferred. Coordinates are the Jewish cemetery at Papiermühlestrasse 112 in Bern-Wankdorf, opened 5 September 1871, which is a separate ground from the Bremgartenfriedhof with which it is sometimes confused.
stops.campa: He is buried beside Maidon in the Jewish cemetery on the Papiermühlestrasse in Bern-Wankdorf, a ground opened in 1871 and separate from the Bremgartenfriedhof with which it is often confused. His parents already lay there from their own Swiss exile, and he had written to the cemetery commission to ask for the place. The man in the grave was a Württemberg manufacturer's son, an American citizen and a German professor twice appointed and once dismissed. None of those came from Switzerland, which is where the endowment had been kept. Pollock is buried in the same ground.

The graves of Rose Horkheimer and Friedrich Pollock in the same ground

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the nineteen volumes
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1985-1996 Fischer edition and its editors; month unknown and defaulted. Posthumous stop, at the Institute pin inherited byte-identical from felix_weil.journey.json.
stops.campa: Alfred Schmidt and Gunzelin Schmid Noerr edit the Gesammelte Schriften for Fischer between 1985 and 1996: nineteen volumes in which the books he published stand next to juvenilia, lecture transcripts, institute memoranda and correspondence he never assembled himself. The critical text of Dialektik der Aufklärung established there is what Edmund Jephcott translates for Stanford in 2002, replacing John Cumming's English of 1972, which the reprints had been issuing since 1979 with Adorno's name moved in front of his.

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the name in the other literature
stops.date_confidence: posthumous reception, not an event in his life; the pin is the Institute's and nothing happened there. The conspiracy tradition itself is attested from Michael Minnicino's 1992 LaRouche-movement essay and William Lind's 1999 documentary and 2000 essay; its content is false as history and is recorded here as tradition, not as fact about Horkheimer.
stops.campa: From 1992 a conspiracy tradition assembled in the LaRouche movement and carried onward by William Lind names Horkheimer personally as the author of a plan: that the Frankfurt School set out to destroy Western civilisation by undermining the family, turning the authoritarian personality into a weapon against conservatives, promoting sexual liberation and silencing the right. The men it describes had fled a totalitarian state that murdered their relatives. His name now circulates in two separate literatures, and the larger of the two is the false one.
suggested_refs: Michael Minnicino, 'The New Dark Age: The Frankfurt School and Political Correctness' (1992)
William Lind's 'Political Correctness: The Frankfurt School' documentary (1999) and essay (2000)

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, Campus Westend: the street renamed
stops.date_confidence: attested for the renaming and the 2015 assignment of addresses on the Campus Westend; month unknown and defaulted. Posthumous stop. The Wuppertal street is recorded as a reconstruction, having only a passing mention.
stops.campa: Goethe University renames the Affensteiner Weg on its Campus Westend the Max-Horkheimer-Strasse, with the addresses formally assigned in 2015; the Bergische Universität Wuppertal has a second one. A plaque marks the Westend flat where he lived. In Stuttgart the city library at the Mailänder Platz keeps a Max-Horkheimer-Kabinett on its third floor, in the section called Leben. The Frankfurt campus that now carries his name is the one the university built on the site of the IG Farben headquarters.
